summit:cfht.title: Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope
summit:cfht.summary: The Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope (CFHT French: Télescope Canada–France–Hawaï) is a 3.58 metres (11.7 ft) optical/infrared telescope located near the summit of Mauna Kea on the Big Island of Hawaiʻi at an altitude of 4,204 m (13,793 ft), within the Maunakea Observatories.

history.text: The Astronomy Precinct was established in 1967 and is located on land protected by the Historical Preservation Act for its significance to Hawaiian culture.
The telescope has a Prime Focus/Cassegrain configuration, and has been in operation since 1979.
As of 2026, however, the project remains on hold pending review of governance and leasing of observatories at this site.

summit:ukirt.title: Maunakea Observatories
summit:ukirt.summary: The Maunakea Observatories (MKO, also known as Mauna Kea Observatories) are a group of independent astronomical research facilities and large telescope observatories that are located at the summit of Mauna Kea on Hawaiʻi, United States.

history.text: The Astronomy Precinct was established in 1967 and is located on land protected by the Historical Preservation Act for its significance to Hawaiian culture.
Until 2014 it was operated by the Joint Astronomy Centre in Hilo and was owned by the United Kingdom Science and Technology Facilities Council.
Decommissioning of UKIRT started on July 7th, 2025.

summit:irtf.title: NASA Infrared Telescope Facility
summit:irtf.summary: The NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (NASA IRTF) is a 3.2-meter (10 ft) telescope optimized for use in infrared astronomy and located at the Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii.

history.text: This requirement has resulted in an instrument which provides spectral resolutions of R~1000-2000 across 0.8-2.4 μm, 2.0-4.1 μm, and 2.3-5.5 μm, using prism cross-dispersers (15 arcsec-long slits).
NSFCam2 was taken off of the telescope in Fall 2012 to upgrade its array to a higher quality engineering grade Hawaii 2RG array with a new array controller.
As of 2019, iSHELL was the second-most heavily used instrument at IRTF (after SpeX). .

summit:subaru.title: Subaru Telescope
summit:subaru.summary: Subaru Telescope (すばる望遠鏡, Subaru Bōenkyō) is the 8.2-metre (320 in) telescope of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, located at the Mauna Kea Observatory on Hawaii.

history.text: In 1984, the University of Tokyo formed an engineering working group to develop and study the concept of a 7.5-metre (300 in) telescope.

In 1985, the astronomy committee of Japan's science council gave top priority to the development of a "Japan National Large Telescope" (JNLT), and in 1986, the University of Tokyo signed an agreement with the University of Hawaiʻi to build…

In 1988, the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan was formed through a reorganization of the University's Tokyo Astronomical Observatory, to oversee the JNLT and other large national astronomy projects.
Construction of the telescope began in April 1991, and later that year, a public contest gave the telescope its official name, Subaru Telescope.
Construction was completed in 1998, and the first scientific images were taken in January 1999.
It had the largest monolithic primary mirror in the world from its commissioning until the Large Binocular Telescope opened in 2005. .

summit:keck.title: W. M. Keck Observatory
summit:keck.summary: Keck Observatory is an astronomical observatory with two telescopes at an elevation of 4,145 meters (13,600 ft) near the summit of Mauna Kea in the U.S. state of Hawaii.

history.text: With a concept first proposed in 1977, telescope designers Terry Mast, of the University of California, Berkeley, and Jerry Nelson of Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory had been developing the technology necessary to build a large, ground-based…
Keck Foundation gave $70 million to fund the construction of the Keck I telescope, which began in September 1985.
First light occurred on November 24, 1990, using 9 of the eventual 36 segments.
When construction of the first telescope was well advanced, further donations allowed the construction of a second telescope starting in 1991.
Both telescopes have 10 m (33 ft) aperture primary mirrors, and, when completed in 1993 (Keck I) and 1996 (Keck II), they were the largest optical reflecting telescopes in the world.
They have been the third and fourth largest since 2006. .

summit:jcmt.title: James Clerk Maxwell Telescope
summit:jcmt.summary: The James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) is a submillimetre-wavelength radio telescope at Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii, US.

history.text: After a series of proposals and debates, in 1975, the SRC millimetre steering committee concluded that it would be possible to construct a 15-metre diameter telescope capable of observing at wavelengths down to 750–800 μm.
Building work started in 1983 and went well.
In 1984, the telescope was shipped from England to Hawaii.
The JCMT started operations in 1987, and was funded until February 2015 by a partnership between the United Kingdom and Canada, and the Netherlands.
In 2013 the Netherlands withdrew, and until 2015 the shares became UK 75 per cent, Canada 25 per cent.
In March 2015 the operation of the JCMT was taken over by the East Asian Observatory.

summit:sma.title: Submillimeter Array
summit:sma.summary: The Submillimeter Array (SMA) consists of eight 6-meter (20 ft) diameter radio telescopes arranged as an interferometer for submillimeter wavelength observations.

history.text: The SMA project was begun in 1983 as part of a broad initiative by Irwin Shapiro, the then new director of the SAO, to produce high resolution astronomical instruments across the electromagnetic spectrum.
A receiver laboratory was established at the SAO's Cambridge location in 1987.

Initially the design called for an array consisting of six antennas, but in 1996 ASIAA joined the project and funded the construction of two additional antennas and the expansion of the correlator to accommodate the near doubling of the…
The SMA was dedicated and began official operations on November 22, 2003. .

summit:vlba.title: VLBA Station Maunakea
summit:vlba.summary: The Maunakea Observatories (MKO, also known as Mauna Kea Observatories) are a group of independent astronomical research facilities and large telescope observatories that are located at the summit of Mauna Kea on Hawaiʻi, United States.

history.text: Significantly predating the current observatories, there is evidence of active astronomy on Mauna Kea in the 1901 Land Office Map of the Island of Hawaii showing the "Hawaii Astronomy Station" near the Mauna Kea summit.
The Astronomy Precinct was established in 1967 and is located on land protected by the Historical Preservation Act for its significance to Hawaiian culture.
By 1970, two 24 in (0.6 m) telescopes had been constructed by the United States Air Force and Lowell Observatory.
In 1973, Canada and France agreed to build the 3.6 m CFHT on Mauna Kea.
This led the Department of Land and Natural Resources to prepare an initial management plan, drafted in 1977 and supplemented in 1980.
In January 1982, the University of Hawaiʻi Board of Regents approved a plan to support the continued development of scientific facilities at the site.

summit:mlo.title: Mauna Loa Observatory
summit:mlo.summary: Mauna Loa Observatory (MLO) is an atmospheric baseline station on Mauna Loa on the island of Hawaiʻi, located in the US state of Hawaii. .

history.text: It was established on the northern flank of Mauna Loa at 3,394 meters (11,134 ft) after 1951–1954 efforts were unable to maintain a summit observatory at 4,100 meters (13,453 ft).
MLO was founded on June 28, 1956, as part of the US Weather Bureau.
Continuous carbon dioxide measurements began in March of 1958 directed by Charles David Keeling from the Scripps Institute of Oceanography.
MLO has been part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Global Monitoring Laboratory (GML)'s Baseline Observatory network since 1972.

The observatory's reading of a historic high in its daily recording of carbon dioxide emissions—400 parts per million, in 2015—was referenced by Pope Francis in his apostolic exhortation on the climate crisis, Laudate Deum. .
The access road was obstructed by lava flow from the 2022 eruption of Mauna Loa.

lco:ogg.title: LCO Haleakalā (Maui)
lco:ogg.summary: Las Cumbres Observatory (LCO) is a network of astronomical observatories run by a non-profit private operating foundation directed by the technologist Wayne Rosing.

history.text: Rosing incorporated Las Cumbres Observatory in 1993 with the goal of aiding universities, observatories, and individuals in the acquisition and improvement of telescopes, optics, and instrumentation.
In 2005, Rosing established the global telescope version of Las Cumbres Observatory.

During 2012 and 2013, nine 1-meter telescopes were constructed and deployed to McDonald Observatory at Fort Davis, Texas; Cerro Tololo Interamerican Observatory (CTIO) in Chile; South African Astronomical Observatory (SAAO), near…
In 2013, a board of directors was established and a president was hired to lead the organization.
Full science scheduling began on 1 May 2014, with the two 2-meter and nine 1-meter telescopes operating as a single, integrated, observatory.
During 2015 and 2016, seven 40-centimeter telescopes were deployed to CTIO, Haleakala Observatory, SSO, and to Teide Observatory on Tenerife in the Canary Islands.

ocean:1617760.title: Hilo Bay tide station
ocean:1617760.summary: A seiche ( SAYSH) is a standing wave in an enclosed or partially enclosed body of water.

history.text: The term was promoted in 1890 by the Swiss hydrologist François-Alphonse Forel, who was the first to make scientific observations of the effect in Lake Geneva.

In 1954, the remnants of Hurricane Hazel piled up water along the northwestern Lake Ontario shoreline near Toronto, causing extensive flooding, and established a seiche that subsequently caused flooding along the south shore.
The massive Good Friday earthquake that hit Alaska in 1964 caused seiches in swimming pools as far away as Puerto Rico.
According to Wilson (1972), this Swiss French dialect word comes from the Latin word siccus meaning "dry", i.e., as the water recedes, the beach dries.
The 1994 Northridge earthquake in California caused swimming pools to overflow across southern California.

Lake seiches can occur very quickly: on July 13, 1995, a large seiche on Lake Superior caused the water level to fall and then rise again by one metre (three feet) within fifteen minutes, leaving some boats hanging from the docks on their…

ocean:1612480.title: Kailua-Kona tide station
ocean:1612480.summary: Hualālai (pronounced [huwəˈlaːlɐi] in Hawaiian) is an active shield volcano on the island of Hawaiʻi in the Hawaiian Islands.

history.text: Between 1700 and 2016, eruptions originated from six vents; four of these lava flows poured into the sea to the west coast. .
Hualālai last erupted in 1800–1801.

Despite maintaining a very low level of activity since its last eruption in 1801, and being unusually inactive for the last 2,000 years, Hualālai is still considered active, and is expected to erupt again sometime in the next 100 years.
The most recent major activity at the volcano was in 1929, when an intense earthquake swarm rocked it, most likely caused by magmatic action near its peak.
This area was explored more closely in a 2001 joint Japan-United States project to explore the volcano's flanks, utilizing the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Kaikō.
This caused $100,000 worth of damage to the Kona district ($1.2 million as of 2010), and two earthquakes with magnitudes of 5.5 and 6.5 were felt as far away as Honolulu.

power:pakinigui.title: Pakini Nui Wind Farm
power:pakinigui.summary: Wind power in Hawaii is produced by the state's 132 commercial wind turbines, totaling 236 MW in capacity.

history.text: The MOD-5B, a 3.2MW wind turbine on Oahu, was the largest in the world in 1987.
These early examples were all out of service by 2010. . . .
In 2012, Hawaii generated 367 million kWh from wind power.
In 2015, wind turbines produced 6.4% of Hawaii's electricity.
Repowered by a new farm at the site in 2017. .
In 2019, Kahuku residents protested the placement of wind towers, leading to hundreds of arrests for obstructing entry of equipment to the turbine sites.

power:hawiwind.title: Hawi Wind Farm
power:hawiwind.summary: Hawi Wind Farm is a wind farm on Upolu Point, the northern tip of Hawaii's largest island, Hawaiʻi.

history.text: On 14 May 2004, Hawaii Electric Light Company (HELCO) bought the project from enXco or EDF Renewable Energy.
Commissioned in 2006, it comprises sixteen 660 kW wind turbines manufactured by Vestas, specifically the Vestas V47 turbine.
In 2011, the Hawi Wind Farm added a 1 megawatt back-up battery system to their wind farm.
However, as recently as 2013 the farm has also had its setbacks.

power:aes-waikoloa.title: AES Waikoloa Solar
power:aes-waikoloa.summary: The energy sector in Hawaii has rapidly adopted solar power due to the high costs of electricity, and good solar resources, and has one of the highest per capita rates of solar power in the United States.

history.text: 16 MW of PV were installed in 2010, 40 MW in 2011, and 109 MW in 2012.
Hawaii had almost 200 MW of grid-connected photovoltaics in 2012.
In 2014, there were over 40,000 rooftop systems, over 10 percent of customers.

Such overbuilding led the Hawaiian Electrical Company (HECO) to stop its net metering program, which reimbursed solar consumers generously for the excess electricity they exported back to the grid, in 2015.
In 2023, distributed solar produced 1,408 GWh while utility-scale solar produced 643 GWh.

The largest utility-scale solar farm in Hawaii is the 60 MW Kuihelani Solar on Maui, which opened in 2024, and includes 240 MWhr of battery storage As of 2024, solar power produced 19.5% of Hawaii's electricity. .

volcano:KWcam.title: Halemaʻumaʻu crater west rim webcam
volcano:KWcam.summary: Kīlauea (US: KIL-ə-WAY-ə, Hawaiian: [kiːlɐwˈwɛjə]) is an active shield volcano in the Hawaiian Islands.

history.text: Western contact and written history began in 1778.

Kīlauea erupted nearly continuously from vents on its eastern rift zone between January 1983 and April 2018, causing major property damage, including the destruction in 1990 of the towns of Kalapana and Kaimū along with the community's…
Between 2008 and 2018, Halemaʻumaʻu, a pit crater located within Kīlauea's summit caldera, hosted an active lava lake.

Beginning in May 2018, activity shifted further downrift from the summit to the lower Puna district, during which lava erupted from two dozen vents with eruptive fountains that sent rivers of lava into the ocean in three places.
Since 2020, several eruptions have occurred within the enlarged Halemaʻumaʻu crater from the 2018 collapse events as well as along the volcano's southwest and east rift zones. .
The most recent eruption began in December 2024, with episodic lava fountains and flows continuing into 2026.

volcano:MKcam.summary: Mauna Loa (, Hawaiian: [ˈmɐwnə ˈlowə]; lit. 'Long Mountain') is one of five volcanoes that form the Island of Hawaii in the U.S. state of Hawaii in the Pacific Ocean.

history.text: Since then, the volcano has remained active, with a history of effusive and explosive eruptions, including 34 eruptions since the first well-documented eruption in 1843. .
Mauna Loa has been monitored intensively by the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory since 1912.
With the assistance of the Buffalo Soldiers in 1915, a path to the top of Mauna Loa was created.

sat:25544.title: International Space Station
sat:25544.summary: The International Space Station (ISS) is a space station in low Earth orbit (LEO).

history.text: The first ISS module was launched in 1998, with major components delivered by Proton, Soyuz and Space Shuttle launch vehicles.
Since 2 November 2000, it has hosted the longest continuous presence of humans in space.
In the 2010 United States National Space Policy, the ISS was given additional roles of serving commercial, diplomatic, and educational purposes. .
On 3 April 2013, scientists reported that hints of dark matter may have been detected by the AMS.
As of August 2025, 290 individuals from 26 countries had visited the station.

After this the ISS is planned to be de-orbited using the US Deorbit Vehicle, but critique of this plan and the proposal of parking the station at a more stable higher orbit has gathered congressional support as of 2026. . .

sat:20580.title: Hubble Space Telescope
sat:20580.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope (HST or Hubble) is a space telescope that was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and remains in operation.

history.text: Its intended launch was in 1983, but the project was beset by technical delays, budget problems, and the 1986 Challenger disaster.
The Hubble Space Telescope (HST or Hubble) is a space telescope that was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and remains in operation.
The optics were corrected to their intended quality by a servicing mission, STS-61, in 1993.
The fifth mission was initially canceled on safety grounds following the Columbia disaster (2003), but after NASA administrator Michael D.
Griffin approved it, the servicing mission was completed in 2009.
Hubble completed 30 years of operation in April 2020 and is predicted to last until 2030 to 2040.

airquality:Hilo.title: Hilo air quality
airquality:Hilo.summary: Hilo (, HEE-low; Hawaiian pronunciation: [ˈhilo]) is the largest settlement in and the county seat of Hawaiʻi County, Hawaii, United States, which encompasses the Island of Hawaiʻi, and is a census-designated place (CDP).

history.text: When William Ellis visited in 1823, the main settlement there was Waiākea on the south shore of Hilo Bay.
For example, by 1887, 26,000 Chinese workers worked in Hawai'i's sugar cane plantations, one of which was the Hilo Sugar Mill.
A breakwater across Hilo Bay was begun in the first decade of the 20th century and completed in 1929.

On April 1, 1946, an 8.6-magnitude earthquake near the Aleutian Islands created a 46-foot-high (14 m) tsunami that hit Hilo 4.9 hours later, killing 159 total in the islands, with 96 deaths in Hilo alone.
In response, an early warning system, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center, was established in 1949 to track these killer waves and provide warning.
The population was 44,186 according to the 2020 census.

airquality:Kailua-Kona.title: Kailua-Kona air quality
airquality:Kailua-Kona.summary: Kailua-Kona is an unincorporated community and, under the name Kailua, a census-designated place (CDP) in Hawaii County, Hawaii, United States.

history.text: The community was established by King Kamehameha I to be his seat of government when he was chief of Kona before he consolidated rule of the archipelago in 1795.
In 1820, the first Christian missionaries arrived and established churches and schools.
As of the census of 2000, there were 9,870 people, 3,537 households, and 2,429 families residing in Kailua-Kona.
Kailua-Kona was the closest major settlement to the epicenter of the 2006 Kiholo Bay earthquake.
In 2014, the Pālamanui Community Forest preserve was created in Kailua-Kona with a goal of preserving and protecting the native trees of Hawai’i. .
Census Bureau significantly altered Kailua CDP's boundaries for the 2020 census.

airquality:Volcano.title: Volcano air quality
airquality:Volcano.summary: A volcano is a vent or fissure in the crust of a planetary-mass object that allows hot lava, volcanic ash, and gases to escape from a magma chamber below the surface.

history.text: National air quality laws have often been effective, notably the 1956 Clean Air Act in Britain and the 1963 US Clean Air Act.
In 2009, a paper was published suggesting a new definition for the word 'volcano' that includes processes such as cryovolcanism.

As of 2023, more than 2.3 billion people in developing countries rely on burning polluting fuels such as firewood, agricultural waste, dry dung, coal, or charcoal for cooking, which causes harmful household air pollution.
